blocks.prompt: 17 (a) An urn contains the first 15 English letters (A-O). Sania is to randomly select 3 letters from the urn. She will win the game if the selected letters are the first three vowel letters. Find the probability of Sania winning the game if: (a) The order of the vowel letters matters
blocks.explanation:
Probability = (winning outcomes) \(\div\) (all outcomes). The first three vowels are A, E, I (all among A-O).
When order matters, outcomes are ordered draws: \({}^{15}P_{3}\).
Plan: count all ordered draws, count the winning one, divide.
steps:
Given: 15 letters A to O; 3 letters drawn; win if they are A, E, I.
To find: the probability of winning when order matters.
Method: \(P = \frac{\text{winning outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}\), every draw equally likely.

Count all ordered draws
\[{}^{15}P_{3} = 15 \times 14 \times 13\]
\[= 2730\]
Why: The first letter can be any of 15, the second any of the remaining 14, the third any of the remaining 13.

Count the winning draws
\[\text{A, then E, then I: } 1\]
Why: When the order of the vowels matters, only the draw in the order A, E, I wins.

Divide
\[P = \dfrac{1}{2730}\]
Why: One winning outcome out of 2730 equally likely outcomes.

Check
\[\dfrac{1}{15} \times \dfrac{1}{14} \times \dfrac{1}{13} = \dfrac{1}{2730} \;\checkmark\]
Why: Draw by draw: A first (1 of 15), then E (1 of 14), then I (1 of 13).

blocks.prompt: 17 (b) An urn contains the first 15 English letters (A-O). Sania is to randomly select 3 letters from the urn. She will win the game if the selected letters are the first three vowel letters. Find the probability of Sania winning the game if: (b) The order of the vowel letters does not matter
blocks.explanation:
Now only the set of 3 letters counts, so outcomes are combinations: \({}^{15}C_{3}\).
Plan: count all selections, count the winning one \(\{A, E, I\}\), divide.
steps:
Given: as in part (a), but the order of drawing does not matter.
To find: the probability of winning.
Method: \(P = \frac{\text{winning outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}\) with outcomes as selections.

Count all selections
\[{}^{15}C_{3} = \dfrac{15 \cdot 14 \cdot 13}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{2730}{6} = 455\]
Why: Each set of 3 letters was counted \(3! = 6\) times in \({}^{15}P_{3}\).

Count the winning selections
\[\{A, E, I\}: 1\]
Why: Only one set of three letters is the set of the first three vowels.

Divide
\[P = \dfrac{1}{455}\]
Why: One winning outcome out of 455 equally likely selections.

Check
\[\dfrac{3!}{2730} = \dfrac{6}{2730} = \dfrac{1}{455} \;\checkmark\]
Why: Counting ordered draws instead, any of the \(3! = 6\) orders of A, E, I wins; the probability is the same.
